title: How can a giant water lily leaf carry so much weight?
hook: The secret is under the leaf, and it inspired a palace of glass.
summary: Thick, air-filled ribs crossing under the leaf spread the load; that design inspired the Crystal Palace.

cardBlocks.text: A giant water lily leaf can be 2 to 3 metres across and yet its blade is only about a millimetre thick. The secret is underwater: the underside of the leaf is covered in thick ribs that branch and cross, forming a network that gives it strength. Inside, the ribs hold air-filled tissue that helps the leaf float.

The underside is also covered in many spines that protect the plant from fish and other animals trying to eat it. The leaf can float a surprising load, but only if the weight is spread evenly over its whole surface.
A giant water lily leaf holds itself up with a network of crossing, air-filled ribs on its underside.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The British gardener and architect Joseph Paxton was the first to make the plant flower in cultivation, in 1849, in a heated pond at Chatsworth. Inspired by the ribs that hold up the leaf, he used a similar cross-braced system for the iron and glass frame of the Crystal Palace, built for the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London.
The plant was named after Queen Victoria, newly crowned in 1837. Three species of giant water lily are known today, all from rivers in tropical South America.
